gameplay_summary: Zelda-like action RPG: as a female soldier from abroad, rescue the princess of Faria from the Wizard's tower, then uncover a deeper plot across towns, an overworld and dungeons, with overhead sword combat.
dossier: Game Arts' action RPG, published in Japan by Hi-Score. gameplay_summary: Kung fu fighting game with RPG elements: in training mode, travel a large map visiting towns, dojos and temples, winning bouts and running errands to learn new techniques, then use your fighter in versus mode.

Beating each castle's master earns a title and a password word, and combining the words leads to the ending. A legendary fighter, Tao Tyler, is a separate goal. gameplay_summary: Command-select text adventure based on the cooking manga Oishinbo: as food journalist Shiro Yamaoka, pick the best choices through three stories about the 'Ultimate Menu', with fifteen ways to fail.
dossier: Shinsei's adventure based on Tetsu Kariya's gourmet manga, with three scenarios built from manga episodes, including one about monkfish liver. Commands include 'chant a spell', 'lie' and 'act stupid', and the fifteen game overs are surreal, such as being arrested for chanting a spell or breaking your arm punching a monkfish. Lines like Yamaoka chanting 'ankimo, ankimo, ankimo!' at a policeman, or 'Yamaoka suddenly seems to hate the world' after he throws his monkfish into the sea, made it a cult kusoge. All the background music is classical.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — A text adventure whose absurd humour and choices are all Japanese text.

gameplay_summary: RPG in a quirky 1980s America: as young Ninten, investigate supernatural events with your great-grandfather's PSI research, gather melodies, fight hippies, zombies and possessed objects with bats and frying pans, and heal with burgers.
dossier: Shigesato Itoi's first MOTHER, developed by Ape and Pax Softnica and Nintendo's only Famicom release of 1989. In the early 1900s, George and Maria vanished from the town of Mother's Day, and only George returned, to pursue strange research. In 1988, their great-grandson is attacked by his own furniture, finds a melody in a music box, and sets out to discover what's behind spreading paranormal events. It deliberately avoids RPG convention: no fantasy kingdom, towns drawn to the same scale as the field, bats, frying pans and air guns for weapons, coins and pendants for armour, junk food for healing, and 'present boxes' for treasure chests. The TV ad's line was 'Don't cry until the ending.' A North American NES version, Earth Bound, was planned but cancelled, and only appeared officially in 2015 as the digital EarthBound Beginnings.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — A dialogue-heavy RPG; Itoi's humour, the story and its clues are Japanese text.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan. A planned NES release as Earth Bound was cancelled; it was later released digitally as EarthBound Beginnings.

gameplay_summary: Cute horror-parody platformer: as resurrected Rick, swing an axe and occasional shotgun through graveyard and haunted stages full of horror-movie send-ups, growing your life bar through experience to rescue Jennifer from the Pumpkin King.

gameplay_summary: Vertical-scrolling helicopter shooter: pilot an attack chopper over ten levels of tanks, battleships and artillery, switching between shot types and using screen-clearing bombs, with a boss at the end of each level.
dossier: CBS/Sony's Famicom port of Toaplan's 1987 arcade Kyuukyoku Tiger, the sequel to Tiger-Heli. You fly through ten increasingly difficult levels of military vehicles, ships and guns, each ending with a boss, and the scenery never stops scrolling until you reach a helipad. nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Twin Cobra (1990).

gameplay_summary: Turn-based space war sim set in the Gradius universe: build battleships and form fleets at your home system, move through warp-linked star systems in production and movement phases, and capture the enemy's home world.
dossier: Konami's space wargame, using the Gradius world and characters (Vic Vipers and Big Cores) but otherwise a standalone game. Its sequel, much later, was the Parodius-flavoured Paro Wars. Each player's home system sits at an end of a map of star systems connected by warp points, from simple layouts to sprawling ones, eight in all. You build warships, form fleets and invade to take the enemy's home planet. Turns alternate, each split into phases such as production and movement. You can play the Bacterion Empire or Gradius, and commanders can move units automatically. The backstory spans centuries of interstellar nations facing an unknown lifeform. It saves to battery. Reviewers' main complaint was slow turns.
language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — The map play is visual, but unit and command menus are Japanese.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Side-scrolling action based on the gag manga Moeru! Oniisan: switch between Kenichi and his friends stage by stage through maze-like warping maps to rescue Yukie from Dora Gon, ending in a Dragon Quest-style command battle.
dossier: Toho's game of Tadashi Sato's Jump gag manga and its anime. Your father Kenkichi gambles Yukie on a dice game before the story starts, and if you win, she isn't kidnapped, the plot never begins and it's game over. From stage 1 the maps are mazes of warps, enemies stream in endlessly from all sides, and with no invincibility after being hit, multiple hits can quickly end the game. The four heroes, Kenichi, Kadou, Rocky and Shiranui, take turns stage by stage. The final fight against Dora Gon switches to a Dragon Quest-style command battle, and the naming jokes follow the manga's crude humour. The NES Circus Caper reworked the theme into a circus rescue, replacing speech bubbles with weapons, reordering stages and removing the credits.
language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — The action is visual, but the opening gamble, the dialogue and the final command battle are Japanese.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Circus Caper (1990), an altered version.
japanese_version_notes: Based on the manga Moeru! Oniisan, with its characters and humour; the NES version replaces the theme with a circus, uses weapons instead of speech bubbles, reorders stages and removes the credits.

gameplay_summary: Mini 4WD board game: roll around a countryside-and-city board buying parts, tune your Tamiya Mini 4WD car, and race in tournaments for points to qualify for and win the Japan Cup.
dossier: Konami's game of the Mini 4WD toy cars that were hugely popular with schoolchildren. It's mainly a board game. A square board has an outer countryside ring and an inner city ring, linked only by train. You move by roulette, up to six spaces a day, and since you can stop it on purpose, the game is nearly impossible if you can't, because you'll never land on the shop you need. Parts tune your car for races, where placing earns points, and enough points get you into the Japan Cup. Events range from comic to absurd, with aliens and gods. Starting cars include the Hotshot, Hornet, Fox, Boomerang, Big Wig and Falcon Jr.

gameplay_summary: Pro wrestling for one or two players: choose from ten international wrestlers with 20+ moves each, grapple by walking into opponents, and pull off signature moves shown in replay cut-scenes, with a play-by-play announcer.
dossier: Tecmo's wrestling game, with ten fictional international wrestlers. It's noted for being the first wrestling game with a play-by-play announcer, Tom Talker (in text bubbles), and perhaps the first with action replays: certain signature moves on a weakened opponent cut to a quick dramatic scene of the move. There's no grapple button. Walking into your opponent starts a grapple, and pad-and-button combinations give each wrestler more than twenty holds and slams, plus ground, running and top-rope attacks. gameplay_summary: Comedy command adventure: as Erika, the ungifted youngest heiress of a zaibatsu, chase stardom with her singing and gather eight allies against the 'Dark Gimmick Army' over five chapters, with song scenes.
dossier: Natsume's comedy adventure for Towa Chiki, built on its Touhou Kenbun Roku system. Commands narrow to the scene, friends give hints, and game overs return you to just before, so it rarely stalls, but it's very short, partly because its large singing-scene graphics used up the space. gameplay_summary: Tax-investigation adventure based on Juzo Itami's film: as inspector Ryoko Itakura, ride the train between areas, explore towns from above and investigate buildings by command menu to expose a tax-evasion ring.

Tax office investigator Ryoko Itakura probes a pachinko parlour's hidden accounts, uncovers a circulating 'tax evasion manual', and follows it to yakuza and a large evasion network. Promoted to the National Tax Agency's investigators (the 'Marusa'), she takes on Hideki Gondo, ending in a raid on his shadow bank. It expands on threads the film leaves vague, and changes details: Gondo is a pure villain, his ex-wife appears, his son is renamed, the informer is different, and her subordinate is the new character Yoshino. gameplay_summary: Virtue-based open-world RPG: rather than defeating a great evil, become the Avatar by mastering eight virtues through your conduct, exploring Britannia, recruiting companions and descending into puzzle-filled dungeons.
dossier: Pony Canyon's Famicom version of Richard Garriott's 1985 Ultima IV, a landmark RPG whose goal isn't to slay a villain but to become a moral exemplar, the Avatar, by living up to eight virtues. On Famicom, the party is limited to four, with the other companions waiting in a room beneath Castle Britannia. Food is gone, items and spells were cut or added, the companion Julia becomes the muscular Julius, and the virtues are reworded more simply, so 'spirituality' becomes 'purity'.

gameplay_summary: Comic horizontal shooter: as the young hermit Mike Chen riding a flying cloud, shoot dumplings, noodles and other Chinese-themed enemies, collect power-ups, and buy special bombs behind doors.

The Famicom version adds an original stage and a hidden stage to the arcade's set, for six stages plus the secret one. Its main 'R.P.G.' mode is a story in which you defeat monsters on the table by hitting them with the ball, power up, earn gold from your score and buy items in shops. Flippers are worked with left on the D-pad and A, up and down moves the flippers' positions, and B nudges the table. Three other modes, a slot-machine table called Circus, a whack-a-mole table called Viva! Golf and the multiplayer Pop! Pop!, can be shared by up to four players taking turns. Reviewers called it one of gaming's most bizarre genre hybrids. A 2024 Jaleco Collection re-release shows your gold at all times.
language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — Pinball is visual, but the RPG mode's story and shop text are Japanese.
nes_counterpart_context: Same game as the NES Pinball Quest (North America 1990).

gameplay_summary: Famista-style baseball with position-specific fielding and arm strength: beat all eleven other teams in a round-robin tournament, play versus, all-stars or watch mode, with diving and leaping catches.
dossier: Tecmo's second 'Gekitou' sports game after its wrestling title. The controls follow Famista and Harikiri Stadium, but it pioneered rating every player's fielding by position (catcher, each infield spot, outfield) along with individual throwing arms, and it lets you leap or dive for fine plays by holding B with a direction. The one-player tournament is a round robin against the other eleven teams, saved by password, with no fixed schedule, though tired pitchers need several games' rest. There's also two-player versus, an all-star game and a watch mode. Holding specific directions on both controllers at reset unlocks a hidden 'ura' mode. Famitsu gave it 25/40.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Baseball is universal; passwords and team names are the only text.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Bad News Baseball (1990).

gameplay_summary: Comedy adventure based on Koji Aihara's animal gag manga: as the bear cub Shiro, chosen by a god to save the forest, travel with Uribo and Choshi-chan to defeat the forest's demon king.
dossier: CBS/Sony's adventure game of Koji Aihara's animal-ecology gag manga about Shiro, a dim-witted white bear cub growing up in the wild with his mother, twin brother and an adopted boar piglet. Here a god picks Shiro as the hero to save the forest, and he sets off with Uribo and Choshi-chan to beat the forest's demon king, meeting the main cast along the way. Jokes and scenes from the manga turn up, but it also adds things the source never had: humanoid characters, gods, man-made objects and animals plainly not from Japan, and the ability to revive creatures from the droppings they became after being eaten. FamiWiki classes it as action-adventure.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — A comedy adventure built on Japanese dialogue and gags.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Survival-horror RPG: five documentary filmmakers trapped in a cursed mansion split into teams, use their unique tools to solve puzzles and survive ghosts with scarce healing, to calm the vengeful spirit of Lady Mamiya.
dossier: Capcom's game of the 1989 horror film Sweet Home, developed alongside it. Thirty years after fresco painter Ichiro Mamiya died, a TV crew (Kazuo, Akiko, Taguchi, Asuka and Kazuo's daughter Emi) goes to his mountain mansion to film his lost frescoes, and Lady Mamiya's ghost seals them in. They can explore alone or in groups of two or three, switching freely. Each has a unique tool needed to finish (camera, lighter, medical kit, lockpick, vacuum cleaner), and items can be dropped and picked up by others. There are no inns to rest at, the dead stay dead, and traps or paralysis can strand a character until rescued. Frescoes hide messages that guide progress. Multiple endings range from all five surviving to only one.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — A puzzle-heavy horror RPG whose clues come from Japanese notes, frescoes and messages.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Baseball with a growth-and-shopping pennant mode: pick six of twelve teams for a 30, 60 or 130-game league, develop players through games, training and items bought with earnings, and win the Japan Series.
dossier: Epoch's first Famicom game, released after it left its own Super Cassette Vision hardware. It borrows the name of Epoch's long-selling Yakyuuban tabletop baseball toy, but nothing else, and it isn't a board game at all. A suit-of-armour 'Baseball Demon', modelled on Daimajin, appears throughout. In the main pennant mode you choose six of twelve teams for a league of 30, 60 or 130 games. Players grow with experience, and post-game earnings pay for special training and items to equip. Win the pennant and you face a random team from the other six in a best-of-seven Japan Series. An open-game mode gives you ¥10 million to spend on items before a single match.
language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — The baseball is visual, but training, shopping and items use Japanese menus.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Block-throwing puzzle: throw your block at matching blocks to clear them, catch the different block it hits in return, and reduce the stack to the target count, across 50 stages plus a fixed-solution Advance mode.
dossier: Taito's Famicom version of its 1989 arcade puzzle game, known abroad as Plotting. Your character moves up and down the side of the stack and throws a block sideways. It falls when it hits a wall, ceiling or pipe. Hitting matching blocks clears them, more at once for more points. When it hits a different block, that block comes back to you as your next throw. A throw that hits a non-matching block clears nothing. The Famicom version has 50 stages with three continues, and a 'reverse' second loop of 200 more, plus an Advance mode of 50 fixed puzzles with limited moves, no timer and unlimited continues. The layout is mirrored compared with the arcade. Famicom Magazine called it very severe.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — A visual puzzle; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: High-school girls' softball: pick a school from one of ten regions and win through regional and national tournaments, then take on a US team, pro baseball sides, retired legends and the major leagues.
dossier: Coconuts Japan's softball game, developed by Marionette, with a ladder that escalates absurdly. You choose one of ten regions of Japan, then one of its six high-school girls' teams. After the regional and national championships you face the American national team, Japanese pro teams (with parody names), a team of retired greats, and finally the major leagues, aiming to be world number one. Games are seven innings with unlimited extras, with a mercy rule at ten runs after six. Losing is game over, but the password shown lets you retry the match. Results appear in a parody of the Pro Yakyuu News TV show, featuring every home-run hitter. Underhand pitches can reach 120 km/h, and the computer is notoriously tough.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Softball is visual; names and the news screen are Japanese but not needed.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Realism-focused baseball supervised by ex-pitcher Takenori Emoto: pick a pitch location then type, and as a batter predict the location and set your timing, with detailed per-player data and team cheering songs.
dossier: Hect's baseball game supervised by former pro pitcher Takenori 'Emoyan' Emoto, one of the earliest games endorsed by a sports commentator. Its title nods to his bestseller on enjoying pro baseball ten times more. Despite the 'Central League edition' subtitle, the team and player names are unlicensed alternatives. It combines Famista-style feel and fielding with Best Play-style detailed player data, and team and star-player cheering songs. At its core is a deeper take on pitch location from Moero!! Pro Yakyuu and Super Real Baseball: pitchers choose a location and then a pitch type, and batters predict where the pitch will go and set their timing. The promised Pacific League edition and a Game Boy '20X' version were cancelled.
language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — The baseball is visual, but the location-and-timing system and data menus are Japanese.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Famista baseball with battery-saved league play: set up leagues of two to six teams over up to 45 games, choose game length, and use new switch-hitters and sidearm pitchers.
dossier: Namco's fifth Famista, the first named for the following year, since Famista '89 had come out only that July. The ROM doubled to 2 megabits, and the series finally got battery backup. New are switch-hitters (previously batters were left or right only) and sidearm pitchers (alongside over- and underhand). Instead of the old elimination format, it introduces league play to the console series for the first time, with two to six teams playing one to nine games per pairing, up to 45 games. Innings can be set to 1, 3, 5 or 9, borrowed from the Game Boy Famista. It has one odd quirk: hard liners from .304-plus hitters dip like topspin, so weaker hitters can drive the ball further. Only in this entry can a ball that hits the backscreen leave a hole.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Baseball is universal; names are Japanese but not needed to play.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Stock-market life sim: grow $500,000 to $1 million on the American stock market to prove yourself worthy of a $600 billion inheritance, spending weekends shopping, dating and buying a house.
dossier: SOFEL's sequel to The Money Game. The hero, Minase in the Japanese version, has to prove he deserves the Benedict family's $600 billion inheritance by turning $500,000 into $1,000,000 through investments in the American stock market. Success brings weekend rewards like shopping trips, dates and big purchases such as a house. The script is by Hiroshi Matsuzawa and the art by manga artist Eiichi Yamagishi (later of Detective Conan special editions). The Japanese and American versions have different storylines, but office layouts and schemes are nearly identical, with only surface changes for North American players; the NES version also has different music. EGM called it one of the most unique RPGs at CES.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — Trading menus, market data and weekend dialogue are all Japanese text.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Wall Street Kid (1990).
japanese_version_notes: The storyline and protagonist differ from the NES version, and the NES music was newly composed by Toshio Murai; office layouts and the scheme are nearly identical.

gameplay_summary: Side-scrolling fantasy action: as a young warrior with a giant axe, cut through monster-ruled lands, charging a power gauge for stronger swings and casting magic, with large sprites and cinematic cut-scenes.
dossier: Jaleco's Famicom version of its 1989 arcade The Lord of King (The Astyanax abroad), made by Aicom on a large cartridge. It keeps the arcade's big characters and adds 'cinema display' story scenes, but its stage layout and story differ substantially from the arcade, and it's one-player only. The axe-wielding hero frees a monster-ruled world. The power gauge rises while you hold off attacking and makes the axe hit harder, until at full power it bursts into flame with greater reach. Magic attacks round out the arsenal.
language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — The action is visual, but the cut-scene story is Japanese.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Astyanax (1990).

gameplay_summary: Two-player co-op beat 'em up: as Billy and Jimmy Lee, avenge Marian's murder through nine stages that go far beyond the arcade, including a moving helicopter, an undersea base and trap rooms.
dossier: Technos Japan's Famicom Double Dragon II, sharing the arcade sequel's title, artwork and premise (Marian has been shot dead by Willy) but largely different in content. Directed by Hiroyuki Sekimoto of River City Ransom, it finally adds two-player co-op, with a mode where the brothers can hit each other. After a first stage loosely based on the arcade's, it heads into its own levels, such as the interior of a moving helicopter, an underwater base and a series of trap rooms, across nine stages. Attacks use left- and right-facing buttons, as in the arcade sequel. The Famicom version lets you play the whole game on any difficulty and balances the settings differently, while the NES version cuts the game short on the easier settings.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Brawling action; the story scenes are Japanese but not needed.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Double Dragon II: The Revenge (1990), an altered version.
japanese_version_notes: The full game is playable on every difficulty, with different difficulty balance; the NES version limits how far you can go on lower settings.

gameplay_summary: Licensed action platformer: as Batman, wall-jump and fight through five levels of Gotham, using batarang, batdisk and batpoon projectiles powered by pellet cartridges.
dossier: Sunsoft's first Batman game, tied to Tim Burton's 1989 film, for which Sunsoft paid about $1 million (¥150 million). The staff even visited the set in London. The story barely resembles the movie, and the five levels run from Gotham's streets to the Axis Chemicals plant and beyond. Unlike Sunsoft's grappling-hook Mega Drive Batman, this one is built around wall jumping, in the vein of Ninja Gaiden, unusual for platformers then. Batman throws batarangs, batdisks and the batpoon, all fuelled by pellet cartridges.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Action platforming; the Japanese cut-scene text is not needed.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Batman: The Video Game (1990).

gameplay_summary: Gothic action platformer prequel: as Ralph C. Belmondo, whip through branching routes across Europe to Dracula's castle, recruiting one of three partners to switch between, with multiple endings.
dossier: Konami's third Famicom Castlevania, the first on cartridge rather than Disk System, and a prequel set centuries before the original. It drops Simon's Quest's RPG elements and returns to stage-by-stage action, but adds branching routes and three possible partners, one of whom can travel with the hero at a time. Your choices lead to multiple endings. Saving is by password. The hero is Ralph C. Belmondo in Japan. The Famicom cartridge's VRC6 chip adds two extra sound channels, which the NES couldn't use, so the western release was rewritten with an MMC5 chip and also changes enemy damage, sprites, backgrounds and effects.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Action platforming; little text, and passwords are visual.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Castlevania III: Dracula's Curse (1990), an altered version.
japanese_version_notes: The VRC6 chip adds two expansion sound channels for a richer soundtrack; the NES version has a reworked soundtrack, different enemy damage, sprites, backgrounds and effects, and the hero renamed Trevor.

gameplay_summary: Time-travel SF adventure starring J-pop group TM Network: thrown back from a 1999 nuclear apocalypse to their 1989 recording studio, work with the band to stop a rogue SDI satellite, with mini-games and a concert finale.
dossier: CBS/Sony's celebrity adventure built around the J-pop group TM Network. On 24 December 1999, the SDI satellite 'Colosseum' runs amok and launches the world's warheads, Earth is destroyed, and the blast throws the hero back to 22 December 1989, two days before its launch, into TM Network's recording studio. Using his future computer MUE as proof, he gets the band to help him stop it, questioning the satellite's developers. It's a pick-a-command, point-at-the-object adventure, and it's harsh: small mistakes and obscure flags end the game, items hide in places that look empty, and 3D mazes and car chases block progress. Chiptune versions of the band's songs play throughout, and the finale recreates a live concert.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — A harsh Japanese text adventure with obscure flags.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Side-scrolling platformer for one or two: as Mappy's son Happy (and rival twin Lappy), collect money across Mappyland to build a house and win the bride Picky, with slot-machine bonus games and shops between stages.
dossier: Namco's sequel to Mappy and Mappyland. Mappy's twin sons Happy and Lappy have grown up, and through Mappy's mistake only one bride candidate, Picky, has been introduced, so they compete for her. She'll only marry the one who builds a house. As in Dragon Buster, you choose areas on a map, collect money and items, and reach the goal, then face Nyamco at a slot machine for prizes you have to win a mini-game to keep. Shops sell items. There's now a life meter. Jumping and then mashing jump lets you hover down by spinning your tail, and kicks defeat enemies and open chests. Alone, an unfinished house means Picky turns you down. With two players, the one who finishes, or has more money, wins, and a perfect tie means she rejects both. Music is by Ako Matsudaira (Atsuko Iwanaga).
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Platforming; shop items are simple to work out.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Greek-myth RPG: as an amnesiac, immortal young man who can survive any fall, follow a recurring dream across the world with companions to stop the last Titan's heir, now the king of darkness.
dossier: Data East's second Glory of Heracles, written by Kazushige Nojima, later of Final Fantasy, and known for its tragic, dramatic story. You aren't Heracles this time. A young man wakes with no memory and an uncanny immortality (he survives any fall), and the only clue to who he is lies in a dream he keeps having. On the way he meets companions such as the deathless acrobat Leion, and learns that the last of the Titans' offspring has crowned himself the king of darkness. Heracles himself joins mid-story. A party system and day-night cycle are new, while most of the first game's quirks were dropped for conventional RPG systems. Some enemies can shatter your weapons and armour in one blow, and fallen allies become angels. Its characters nod to The Wizard of Oz.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — A story-driven RPG; the tragic plot and its clues are Japanese text.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Rugby game for one or two players, the Famicom's only rugby title; the sources give no further gameplay detail.

gameplay_summary: Comic Edo-flavoured RPG: as the noble thief Goemon with self-styled ninja of justice Ebisumaru, travel Japan's towns and dungeons in turn-based battles to recover the stolen family heirloom, the golden kiseru.
dossier: Konami's first Ganbare Goemon RPG, a 'gaiden' break from the action series that brought in comic touches the later games kept. Back in Hagure Town after a long journey, Goemon finds the family heirloom, a golden kiseru pipe, missing from his shrine, a case of 'the thief's house got burgled'. As he packs to go after it, the self-proclaimed 'ninja of justice' Ebisumaru turns up and insists on coming. It's a standard command RPG with a world map, towns, dungeons, random encounters and turn-based fights. Battles show a status panel with faces that react to damage and victory, and every enemy is animated and unique (apart from the San-Ninja trio), a large bestiary for a Famicom RPG. It's included in the 2026 Ganbare Goemon Daishuugou! collection.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — A Japanese-text RPG full of comic dialogue.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Room-by-room Eggerland puzzle: as Lolo, collect every Heart Framer in each of 50 rooms by pushing Emerald Framers and egging enemies, to rescue Lala from King Egger, plus hidden Pro rooms.
dossier: HAL's Famicom Adventures of Lolo, which carries the Eggerland rules and characters over, and which the NES released as Adventures of Lolo 2. It has 50 puzzle rooms ending with King Egger, plus four hidden 'Pro' rooms for experts. The puzzles are compiled from Eggerland: Meikyuu no Fukkatsu and Eggerland: Souzou he no Tabidachi, with some monsters redrawn and new, harder rooms. Famicom Magazine called it the most beautifully laid out game in the series, and Famitsu awarded it Silver (30/40). A Famicom Adventures of Lolo II followed in December 1990, regarded as the series' hardest.

nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Adventures of Lolo 2 (1990).

gameplay_summary: Two-player run-and-gun sequel: as Bill and Lance, fight possessed troops and mutated aliens in side-scrolling and overhead stages, shooting capsules for stackable weapon upgrades.
dossier: Konami's Famicom version of its 1988 arcade Super Contra, without the 'Alien no Gyakushuu' subtitle. The pseudo-3D stages are gone. gameplay_summary: Poker falling-card puzzle: drop cards into a grid to form poker hands in rows and columns, clearing them to work through the deck.
dossier: Hect's poker-themed falling puzzle game. gameplay_summary: Sengoku grand strategy with retainer generals: as a daimyo, use strategic commands for development, trade, diplomacy and intrigue, and fight day-and-night battles and sieges to unify Japan.
dossier: Koei's Famicom port of the third Nobunaga's Ambition (1988), produced by Kou Shibusawa with music by Yoko Kanno and Mitsuo Yamamoto. Borrowing from Romance of the Three Kingdoms, it introduces subordinate generals to the series, along with day and night in battle and siege warfare. Tohoku and Kyushu are left off the map. Strategic commands cover movement, development, trade, intelligence, personnel, diplomacy, intrigue and military affairs, and battle commands include move, attack, wait, retreat, intelligence and messengers. Each map turn is a season and each battle turn a day, and victory can come from rout, destroying the enemy command unit and other means. Computer Gaming World praised its improved AI. The NES version was reissued in Console Archives in 2026.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — Strategy menus, generals and reports are all Japanese text.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Nobunaga's Ambition II (1991).

gameplay_summary: Side-scrolling action from the Abunai Deka film: as detectives Taka and Yuji, alone or together, fight through nine stages of hitmen while bringing down the Ginseikai crime syndicate.
dossier: Toei Animation's game of the 1989 film Mottomo Abunai Deka, from the Abunai Deka cop series. You pick Taka or Yuji, or two players control both at once. Stages scroll right but let you backtrack, and each ends at a goal or boss, nine in all. It was poorly received: Famitsu gave it 16/40.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Action; the Japanese story text is not needed to play.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Five-chapter RPG: play separate stories of different characters before the Chosen Hero gathers them, with AI-controlled allies, a wagon for extra party members, and a hot-air balloon.
dossier: The fourth Dragon Quest, the last on the Famicom and the start of the Zenithian trilogy. Each chapter stars different characters starting from level 1, before the fifth brings in the Hero (whose name and sex you choose) to gather the Chosen. New systems include AI tactics that control your allies in battle, and a wagon that lets you bring along more than four companions and swap them in, so the Hero needn't even be in the active party. Day and night, ships, a hot-air balloon, three tiers of keys and travel doors also feature.

nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Dragon Warrior IV (1992).

gameplay_summary: Rolling Thunder-style action: as special forces agent 'Viper', infiltrate seven South American drug-syndicate hideouts, leaping between floors, ducking into doors for items, and rescuing a captured agent in each.
dossier: Capcom's action game, developed by Arc System Works, in the mould of Namco's Rolling Thunder. In each of its seven hideouts he rescues a missing agent and finds clues to the real mastermind. As in Rolling Thunder, holding up or down with jump moves you between floors, and doors hold power-ups or let you dodge enemies. You carry a pistol or a fully automatic machine gun, with pickups for ammo, health, extra time and lives. Famitsu gave it 24/40.

nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Code Name: Viper (1990).

gameplay_summary: Licensed action game based on the Kiteretsu anime: as young inventor Kiteretsu, escape the world of the Dream Mirror, creating inventions by button-mashing while recruited friends follow you as extra hit areas.
dossier: Epoch's game of the Fujiko F. Fujio anime about boy inventor Kiteretsu and his robot Korosuke. The cast are pulled into the world of the 'Yumemi Kagami' (dream-viewing mirror) and have to escape. The maps are monotonous rows of psychedelic tiles. You build inventions by mashing buttons, and the friends who join you don't fight at all. They just add more hitboxes behind you, making them a liability, an odd design that got the game noticed. To continue, you have to take out a 'loan' with the 'Kiteretsu Jigoku' invention you build early on.
language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — The action is visual, but the inventions and continue system involve Japanese text.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: RPG based on the 1989 Akuma-kun anime: travel the world to defeat Toukaku Taitei, who plans to conquer it, meeting demons from Shigeru Mizuki's series, with a 61-character password.
dossier: Bandai's RPG of the 1989 anime of Shigeru Mizuki's Akuma-kun, about a genius boy who calls on demons to bring peace to the world. Apart from the final boss being Toukaku Taitei, the would-be world conqueror, the story is almost entirely original and spans the whole world. Few of the series' demons appear: Cerberus is the first mid-boss and others turn up as ordinary encounters. Some enemies, such as Backbeard and a poltergeist, appear only here, and the wizard Satan from the Ichiro Matsushita version figures in the plot. Progress is saved with a long password using 61 hiragana plus numerals.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — A Japanese-text RPG with a long hiragana password.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.
